title: Parallel Programming
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of parallel programming in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply parallel programming to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: Parallel Programming is lesson 141 in Asynchronous Programming and Concurrency. Asynchronous methods let a caller await an operation without blocking a thread during I/O. Concurrency, parallel execution, and thread safety solve different problems.
content.why_it_matters: Asynchrony improves responsiveness; it does not automatically make CPU work faster or shared state safe. This lesson focuses on parallel programming and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for parallel programming. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Parallel loops
items.text: Check initialization, termination, and progress together; every loop needs a clear path to completion or cancellation.

items.title: Parallel LINQ
items.text: Break the query into readable stages and verify the source, predicate, projection, ordering, and materialization point.

items.title: CPU-bound parallel tasks
items.text: Await I/O-bound tasks, pass cancellation tokens across boundaries, and protect shared mutable state explicitly.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates parallel programming. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates parallel programming rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for parallel programming before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
